item.title: Statistics: Credible vs. Confidence Intervals — Daily Learning
item.description: After a quarterback's first 40 throws, a model might put his true completion rate between 58% and 68%, and as a 95% credible interval that means you are 95% sure his true rate is in there. The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the…
item.content:encoded: After a quarterback's first 40 throws, a model might put his true completion rate between 58% and 68%, and as a 95% credible interval that means you are 95% sure his true rate is in there. The confidence interval from the same data can look identical on paper, yet it answers a different question: if you repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the true value.

item.title: Big Idea: The Simulation Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument is that a posthuman civilization could run so many detailed simulations of conscious minds that the simulated would vastly outnumber the real. That leaves three options: humanity goes extinct before reaching that stage, posthumans almost never run such simulations, or we are almost certainly living in one.

item.title: Big Idea: The Gettier Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: In June 1963, Edmund Gettier argued in a three-page paper that justified true belief is not enough for knowledge. item.title: Statistics: Publication Bias - Daily Learning
item.description: Publication bias, as Scribbr defined it in October 2022, is what happens when exciting, positive results get published while null or boring ones stay unpublished in a drawer, the file-drawer problem. Imagine 20 labs test a useless betting system and, by chance, one finds a “significant” edge, and only that study gets published, so readers see a system that works.

item.title: Statistics: The Kelly Criterion — Daily Learning
item.description: The Kelly criterion sizes a bet from your edge and the odds, so a 55% chance at even money calls for 10% of your bankroll. Because that 55% is only an estimate, half-Kelly keeps about 75% of the growth while roughly halving the swings.

item.title: Big Idea: The Grandfather Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: If you go back before your grandfather has children and stop him from having any, you are never born, so nobody goes back to stop him. The ways out are a fixed timeline, where the attempt must fail, or a branching one, where you arrive in a timeline without you.

item.title: Big Idea: The Ultimatum Game — Daily Learning
item.description: In a 2009 paper on experiments around the world, one player proposes a split of $100 and the other can reject it and leave both with nothing, yet people routinely reject offers below roughly 20–30% rather than accept an unfair split. What is the smallest split you would accept, and what does that number say about you?

item.title: Statistics: The Prosecutor's Fallacy — Daily Learning
item.description: The prosecutor's fallacy is confusing the chance of seeing this evidence if someone were innocent with the chance they are innocent given that evidence. A 1-in-a-million DNA match sounds like near-certain guilt, but in a city of 10 million you would expect about 10 innocent matches by chance alone.

item.title: Big Idea: The Münchhausen Trilemma — Daily Learning
item.description: The Münchhausen Trilemma says every attempt to justify a belief ends in an infinite regress of reasons, a circle in which the conclusion supports itself, or an arbitrary stopping point where you declare something true without proof. The honest move is to name your starting points, your priors, and let evidence move them when they fail.

The honest move is to name your starting points, your priors, and let evidence move them when they fail.

item.title: Statistics: The Law of Large Numbers — Daily Learning
item.description: The more times you repeat something, the closer your observed average drifts toward its true long-run average. A bettor with a true 55% win rate might win only 4 of their first 10 bets, yet over 1,000 bets that rate tends to sit close to 55%, which is why casinos and sharp bettors trust volume over single outcomes.
